cells.tense: You're seeing clearly what's finished and what isn't, and your hands are steady on the part that stays.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're keeping through this clearing, write what it gives you on a note, and leave the note where you'll see it tomorrow.
cells.core:
The clearing is underway and you're not fighting it. You can tell what's over from what's still yours, and you tend what stays the way you've tended it all along — on time, without being asked, without announcements. What you're keeping alive is alive because you kept it. Growth here doesn't need forcing; it needs one honest sentence about who did the keeping.

Name one thing you're keeping through this clearing, write what it gives you on a note, and leave the note where you'll see it tomorrow. What you gain is a record of your own care, and that written line is something a quiet hand rarely gets otherwise.

cells.tense: You're living past the clearing — planning the bare floor before anything's actually been moved out.
cells.ask: Pick one ending you keep rehearsing, do one physical act to move it along — pack the box, delete the file — and then leave that ending alone for a week.
cells.core:
You're ahead of the room you're standing in. The end gets scripted before it happens, the conversation gets rehearsed, things on their way out get tended as if they were staying — and the energy goes into a picture that hasn't arrived. What's finished needs room to finish on its own clock. Hands that are in it early are hands that can't hold the rest.

Pick one ending you keep rehearsing, do one physical act to move it along — pack the box, delete the file — and then leave that ending alone for a week. What you get back is a day that arrives instead of one you already spent, and the clearing finishes without you forcing the clock.

cells.tense: You're still standing in last season's room, and your hands haven't touched what's waiting to be cleared.
cells.ask: Open one stuck drawer or box, take out a single object that belonged to what's over, and put it by the door.
cells.core:
The clearing is waiting and your hands aren't in it. Papers stack, shelves fill, the same decision gets postponed — not because you don't know, but because touching it would say so out loud. What you keep, you keep quietly, and then can't say what any of it is for now. None of that is a verdict on you; it's what under-tending looks like from the inside.

Open one stuck drawer or box, take out a single object that belonged to what's over, and put it by the door. One object starts the rest of it moving, and nothing today has to get decided all at once — a small light followed is enough to get your hands back in the room.

cells.tense: You're doing the clearing and talking about it like weather — the work is happening and your name isn't on it.
cells.ask: Say one sentence to one person: what you're in the middle of ending and that it's heavy — nothing after that sentence.
cells.core:
The clearing is happening and you keep the credit off yourself. You drop a commitment, draw a line, let something end — and describe it as what's needed, or what anyone would do in your spot. The effort is real and the call was real, and it gets filed under circumstances instead of under the person actually carrying it. Say it once to someone and it stops being ambient.

Say one sentence to one person: what you're in the middle of ending and that it's heavy — nothing after it. Company is what's available on the other side of that sentence, and the weight gets a witness instead of staying something only the room knows about.
